newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Two Chicago ghetto kids reveal their reality in book.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Two Chicago ghetto kids reveal their reality in book.

text.p: If President Bill Clinton had read "Our America" written by two teenagers from Chicago's ghetto before he made his race relations speech last month, he might have decided to mobilise Americans to change the living conditions that divide the nation right away rather than just discussing them for a year.

Written with the aim of sparking a new war against urban poverty and crime, the book, fully titled "Our America: Life and Death on the Southside of Chicago," is the third collaboration by LeAlan Jones and Lloyd Newman, both 18, and David Isay, who discovered them when they were 13-year-olds.

"We're on a mission to let people know what the situation is because their community is so isolated," Isay told Reuters during a book tour stop in Washington. "I hope people read the book, throw it across the room, slam it against the wall and get furious about the situation."

"I hope that our readers can gain an understanding of the environment from which we come. We talk about wanting to help one another, but if they don't know the situation how can they help?" Jones asked.

The three first met when Isay, an independent radio producer, was asked to work on a documentary examining race and ethnicity in Chicago. In an effort to do something different, he chose the two 13-year-olds to report on their lives in the Ida B. Wells housing project for a week.

The first section of "Our America" was drawn from interviews and conversations collected for the radio documentary entitled "Ghetto Life 101," which aired on National Public Radio (NPR) in 1993 and won several awards.
GUNS, DRUGS, VIOLENCE AND DEATH ARE ROUTINE

Through their brutally honest reporting, Jones and Newman force readers to face the reality of a community where guns, drugs, alcohol, theft, violence and death are routine. They introduce "the other America" to a life where children cannot cross an open field for fear of getting shot, where many people believe they will be dead in ten years, where a typical 17-year-old has 30 to 40 close friends who have been killed, where children come to school bleary-eyed, their sleep disturbed by the sound of gunshots all night.

"In Vietnam, them people came back crazy. I live in Vietnam, so what you think I'm gonna be if I live in it and they just went and visited? Living around here is depressing!" the young reporters wrote.

"You might not want to invite us to your parties, you might think we'll rob you blind when you got your back turned, but ... don't look at us like we're an alien or an android or an animal or something ... we're human," Jones said, speaking for them both.

More than a year after the 1993 broadcast, the duo were on assignment again, reporting on a tragic incident involving 5-year-old Eric Morse, who was pushed out of a window on the fourteenth-floor by two older boys after he refused to steal candy for them. The murder occured right behind Jones' house.

The second section of "Our America" is based on their documentary "Remorse: The 14 Stories of Eric Morse," which ran on NPR in 1996 and won a string of prizes including the Peabody Award and the Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award.

While newspapers and television networks covered the story superficially, Jones and Newman said, they examined every angle of the case, interviewing defence and prosecution attorneys, neighbours, friends, local police and family members of the victim and the perpetrators.

In answer to those who ask how children can commit such heinous crimes, Jones and Newman said their reporting revealed that when adults are themselves involved in theft, violence and murder there is no one to teach the young even the basic principles of what is right and wrong.

After four years of reporting, they are eager to succeed in life and want to concentrate on their studies. Both say success to them is not about money or status but about getting out of the housing project. Jones, who will attend Florida State University, and Newman, who will finish high school, are determined to come back to Ida B. Wells as role models.

"To come out of where I live I think is more than success. I think you earn a medal," Newman said. "(I want to) show the other children there is another way up besides doing negative things ... and show them what I've become."

Jones, Newman and Isay hope their book will anger readers into joining in their war against deplorable conditions in ghettos around the country. As Isay said, the two teenagers have proven that "if you give them a chance, if you give them an opportunity ... they're going to do wonderful things."
